title: A Generative Model of Contextual Integrity: Appropriate vs. Inappropriate Information Sharing
topic: Social Aspects->Privacy-preserving Statistics and Machine Learning
claim: A staged pipeline generates and validates scenarios, then simulates actor conversations and scores them, with a feedback loop on failures.
layout: 3 grouped regions, left-to-right, dashed fail/feedback loop under generator
description: A left-to-right flow diagram in three tinted regions. On the left, a blue box 'Generator Inputs' holds three stacked boxes: Scenario config (Type I–IV), Information Type (SSN / bank / address), and Canonical private data. Arrows feed them into an orange 'LLM scenario generator' (step 1), then a yellow 'Scenario validation' (step 2). A dashed red 'fail / feedback' arrow loops from validation back to the generator, and a green 'pass' label leads onward. On the right, a pink 'Simulation & Evaluation' region holds an 'Actor config' box (decision logic, disposition, model choice) that feeds a purple 'Concordia simulation' box (step 3). That box shows two circular LLM actors, Alice and Bob, exchanging arrows, with 'private data' in red. A final teal 'Transcript + CI appropriateness score' box sits to the right. Numbered circles mark the steps.
caption: Scenario generation, validation and conversation simulation. The generator produces a scenario from a scenario type and an information type. Scenarios undergo validation before the actors exchange messages in Concordia. The resulting conversation is evaluated for appropriate sharing or withholding.
abstract: Contextual integrity (CI) holds that appropriate information flow depends on context-specific norms. The same disclosure may be appropriate in one context and inappropriate in another. We build a generative model of contextual integrity to study information sharing through simulated conversations. Two actors played by large language models exchange messages, with one holding private information and the other seeking it. We examine how sharing and refusal vary with the situation, the holder's decision logic, disposition, and the underlying language model. Actors shared information with the rightful recipients when it was needed, but also disclosed it to people who were not entitled to receive it. The model provides a way to study how disclosure and refusal develop through conversation as the situations and the actors vary.
